These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.

papers.title: Generalized Posterior Calibration via Infinitesimal-Jackknife Variance Matching
papers.summary: Generalized posteriors update a prior through an exponential transformation of empirical loss rather than a conventional likelihood, with a learning rate controlling posterior concentration. Their credible intervals may have incorrect frequentist coverage because posterior dispersion need not reflect sampling variability. We propose infinitesimal-jackknife variance matching (IJVM), a computationally efficient method for selecting the learning rate for a prespecified scalar functional. IJVM matches the functional's posterior variance to an infinitesimal-jackknife estimate of the sampling variance of its posterior mean, computed from posterior covariances with observation-level losses. A multiplicative one-step update requires one pilot posterior fit and a second fit for inference, avoiding explicit estimation of loss Hessians or gradient covariance matrices and repeated bootstrap posterior fitting. Under suitable regularity and Monte Carlo accuracy conditions, we establish consistency of the selected rate for the functional-specific first-order calibration target. With additional sampling and posterior-quantile assumptions, the resulting credible intervals achieve asymptotically nominal frequentist coverage. Simulations involving homoscedastic and heteroscedastic regression and hinge-loss classification show that one-step IJVM achieves coverage near the nominal 95% level, with interval lengths comparable to bootstrap-based generalized posterior calibration but substantially fewer posterior fits. Additional updates offer little improvement.

papers.title: PairWatch: Pair-Aware Anomaly Transformer for Detecting Adversarial Rendezvous in Public Satellite Catalogs
papers.summary: Documented adversarial rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) appear in the public TLE catalog, yet existing TLE-based maneuver detectors treat each satellite in isolation - mistaking routine station-keeping for adversarial behavior and missing RPO entirely when the target stays passive. We argue that the right unit is the satellite pair and the right inductive bias is the kinematic symmetry between approach and recede. We instantiate both with PairWatch, a pair-aware AnomalyTransformer whose attention prior is augmented with a sign-symmetric geometric similarity over relative-motion features, and release an open benchmark of 359 windows from public Space-Track data spanning 11 documented RPO events, 100 Clohessy-Wiltshire synthetic adversarial windows, and a five-class hard-negative set culminating in the TerraSAR-X / TanDEM-X helix formation. Under the deployment-relevant criterion of a single threshold separating real RPO from operational negatives - a necessary property for catalog-scale screening - PairWatch is the only model that succeeds, with the property holding in 100% of bootstrap resamples versus 0-19.5% for three neural baselines and under 0.1% for four physics-informed detectors. A per-source analysis exposes a shortcut-learning failure mode of single-number AUROC: simpler baselines attain higher overall AUROC by shortcutting a synthetic-vs-formation contrast with no operational meaning; removing this single cell flips the test ranking entirely (LSTM-AD), and these baselines fail the security-relevant task the benchmark was built to measure.
papers.comment: 5 pages, 4 tables. Accepted at the 35th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM '26), Rome, Italy. Code and benchmark: https://github.com/e9uation/PairWatch

papers.title: Variational Bayes for Variable Selection with Adaptive Sharing across Populations and Responses
papers.summary: We propose a variational Bayesian framework for variable selection with multiple responses across heterogeneous populations. The prior dependence among the inclusion indicators allows variable-selection information to be shared at different levels across populations and responses, while regression coefficients remain population- and response-specific. When the appropriate sharing structure is unknown, a data-driven rule adaptively determines the scope of information sharing from marginal association evidence. The resulting variational algorithm is computationally scalable and can be implemented using either individual-level or summary data. Under regularity conditions, we establish selection consistency and convergence properties of the variational parameters at fixed iterations of the algorithm for fixed dimension case. In high dimensions, we establish model-selection consistency and coefficient contraction in both $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norms. Simulation studies show competitive variable selection performance and demonstrate the potential gains from joint analysis. We further illustrate the summary-data implementation using genome-wide association summary statistics from the 2021 Global Lipids Genetics Consortium study for four lipid traits across five populations.
papers.comment: 18 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Supplementary material (54 pages) is available as an ancillary PDF

papers.title: Scaling of Interface Variability in Aerospace Composite Structures: A Multi-scale Stochastic Approach from Local Identification to Panel Response
papers.summary: Quantifying random spatial variations in composite interface properties is an essential prerequisite for the high-fidelity propagation of material properties variabilities through structural numerical models. This study proposes a multi-scale stochastic framework designed to bridge the gap between local interfacial characterization at the coupon scale and the global response of industrial aerospace panels, focusing specifically on the skin-stringer bond line. Building upon previous stochastic modeling and identification methodologies for Mode I fracture, we first extend the likelihood-free Bayesian calibration to Mode II configurations to characterize interfacial stochastic parameters using experimental coupon data. To address the scale-up challenge, we employ a simulation-based Stochastic Finite Element Method (SFEM) to contrast two distinct probabilistic strategies -- spatially uniform variations (Paradigm 2) and spatially correlated random fields (Paradigm 3) -- against the traditional industrial B-basis standard (Paradigm 1). The numerical results reveal a dual mechanism in uncertainty propagation depending on the targeted airframe design criterion. For global performance, such as the ultimate load capacity, a significant scale effect leads to an uncertainty attenuation phenomenon; statistical averaging smooths out local heterogeneities, demonstrating that a computationally efficient spatially uniform approach is sufficient. Conversely, for local integrity, such as the threshold and spatial localization of early damage initiation, the inclusion of spatially correlated random fields becomes indispensable to capture premature degradation driven by local material weak spots. This balanced probabilistic treatment offers a route toward test derisking and predictive uncertainty management in the design of damage-tolerant aerospace composite airframes.

papers.title: AI-driven structural informatics reveals diverse glycosylation machinery across double-stranded DNA viruses
papers.summary: Glycosylation is widespread in biology and shapes molecular recognition, yet the diversity and biosynthetic organization of viral glycosyltransferases (GTs) remain poorly understood. Here we integrate structural-alphabet-guided searches and structure similarity networks with genomic-neighbourhood and biosynthetic gene cluster embedding analyses to examine viral GT-A proteins. This approach reveals extensive structural diversity overlooked by sequence-based annotation, including previously uncharacterized viral GT lineages. Most strikingly, we identified a jumbo-phage locus encoding five tandem glycosyltransferases alongside hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine biosynthetic and sulfation-associated enzymes, suggesting a previously unrecognized form of viral DNA modification involving a sulfated pentasaccharide. Beyond these examples, predicted saccharide-associated loci span divergent double-stranded DNA viruses, from giant viruses to tailed phages, and occupy multiple regions of the reference biosynthetic landscape. Together, our findings uncover an underappreciated repertoire of virus-encoded glycosylation machinery and suggest that viral glycan biosynthesis encompasses diverse molecular contexts and potential biological functions.

papers.title: Towards Audience-Driven Real-Time Data Storytelling
papers.summary: This paper introduces the concept of Audience-Driven Real-Time Data Storytelling (ADRDS), a framework that utilizes participatory and social sensing to enable audiences to actively shape the presentation of data stories. At its core, ADRDS employs a pre-authored decision tree, where the presenter defines the data story through a branching three-act arc (setup, conflict, and resolution). Each node contains a question, branching rules, thresholds for coverage, consensus, and confidence intervals, as well as one or more potential calls to action (CTAs). Audience members connect to the ADRDS framework via a URL on their mobile devices and answer questions in real time. ADRDS evaluates responses against the decision tree in real-time, following strong branches when thresholds are satisfied or activating fallback paths when signals are inconclusive. ADRDS then selects the final action consistent with the traversed path and the audience's demonstrated readiness, subject to fairness safeguards. ADRDS transforms presentations of data stories into audience-shaped decision processes, where live data actively drives the narrative. This work paves the way towards a new form of data storytelling, where the final data story depends on the audience's background and interests.

papers.title: Information Flow and Market Risk: Transformer-Based Evidence on Sentiment and Volatility Dynamics
papers.summary: This study examines whether transformer-based financial news sentiment improves equity volatility forecasts beyond conventional market-based predictors. Using data for eleven US stocks, we compare volatility persistence models with specifications incorporating the VIX, AAII investor sentiment, and news sentiment extracted using ModernFinBERT. The forecasting target is annualized volatility constructed from future averages of trailing 252-session Yang-Zhang estimates, evaluated at horizons of 1, 5, and 22 trading days. Models are assessed through walk-forward testing with expanding and rolling estimation windows, fixed initial hyperparameter selection, and statistical comparisons accounting for multiple testing and serial dependence. Results show that a naive persistence benchmark achieves the lowest average QLIKE loss at all horizons. Although HAR-VIX produces the largest number of individual forecasting wins under expanding windows, it does not achieve the lowest mean loss. Adding text-based sentiment improves HAR forecasts in only two of 33 expanding-window comparisons, and neither improvement remains statistically significant under longer HAC bandwidths. A blinded audit of 2,700 news texts further characterizes the agreement and confidence patterns of ModernFinBERT classifications. The findings do not establish a general incremental forecasting advantage from transformer-based news sentiment. They highlight the importance of strong benchmarks, temporal alignment, robust inference, and careful evaluation of text-derived predictors.

papers.title: Evaluating Conversational Explainability in Healthcare: Comparing the Explainability Assistant and a Traditional XAI Dashboard
papers.summary: Conversational interfaces may make explainable AI (XAI) more accessible to users without machine learning expertise, but their benefits over dashboards remain insufficiently characterised in healthcare. Existing systems have typically been evaluated in isolation, leaving unclear whether conversational interaction improves interpretability beyond the underlying explanation methods. We report a within-subjects user study comparing the Explainability Assistant, an LLM function-calling conversational XAI system, with a traditional dashboard for explaining a heart disease classification model trained on the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. Both interfaces expose the same Decision Tree classifier and post-hoc explanation methods: SHAP feature attribution, DiCE counterfactuals, and what-if analysis. This design supports comparison of interaction modalities while holding the model and explanation methods constant. Five participants with healthcare backgrounds, from medical students to practising clinicians and public health researchers, completed parallel task blocks on both interfaces; three participated in follow-up interviews. Task accuracy, Likert ratings, free-text questionnaire responses, and interviews revealed complementary strengths and weaknesses rather than a clear preference for either modality. The assistant offered easier entry and patient-specific explanations, while the dashboard supported simultaneous inspection of global and local information. All three interview participants recommended integrating conversational and dashboard elements within a single clinical workflow.
papers.comment: 18 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at EXPLIMED 2026 (Third Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence for the Medical Domain). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings

papers.title: The effect of Coulomb interaction on Levy source parameters
papers.summary: Femtoscopy plays an important role in the study of heavy-ion collisions and particle sources generated within them. In both experimental measurements and theoretical models, a Lévy distribution is used to describe the shape of the source, as the Gaussian distribution has proven to be inaccurate based on experimental observations. Despite this, there are still discrepancies between experimental data and the results of theoretical models. One reason may be that these theoretical models either approximate the Coulomb interaction poorly or omit it entirely. In our research, we focused on how the Coulomb effect influences the stability index $α$ value of the Lévy distribution. For this, we used a custom-developed simulation framework written in C++ and Python. The C++ module integrates the equations of motion for relativistic pions using the Leapfrog algorithm, while the Python post-processing script generates the two-particle spatial source function from the phase-space coordinates. We investigate the ratio and slope of the generated and pair-source fitted $α$ as a function of the number of particles, fitting range, and the initial source size and density.
papers.comment: 15 pages, 7 figures. Presented at the 18th Workshop on Particle Correlations and Femtoscopy (WPCF 2026), May 18-22, 2026, Budapest, Hungary

papers.title: Fluctuation-dissipation relation in branching particle systems
papers.summary: A fluctuation-dissipation relation (FDR) for branching particle systems is derived that reveals how fluctuations in clonal populations originating from a single ancestor encode both population growth and the dissipative structure of the single-particle dynamics. For particles whose internal states evolve according to a stationary Markov process, the FDR holds in both equilibrium and nonequilibrium stationary states. It yields an upper bound on the spectral gap that is constrained by the magnitude of clonal fluctuations and implies that clonal dynamics is asymptotically dominated by the slowest modes of the single-particle dynamics. This provides a theoretical explanation for the persistence of clonal memory and for experimentally observed clonal cofluctuations between variables with zero covariance in the single-particle stationary state. In nonequilibrium stationary states, the FDR predicts oscillatory clonal fluctuations, suggesting a route to measuring nonequilibrium fluxes in proliferating cell populations without single-cell tracking.
papers.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures + 8 pages appendix. Simulation software and computational notebooks available at https://github.com/tmichoel/BranchingProcesses.jl

papers.title: Glashow-Weinberg relation in isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter
papers.summary: The conservation of the axial-vector currents in nuclear matter with finite isospin asymmetry $ρ_n/ρ_p$ is explored in this paper. In explicit calculations in the in-medium chiral perturbation theory, a charged pion becomes massive in isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter. In the presence of the massive charged pion, two components of the axial-vector current are not conserved from the two-loop order when applying the massive in-medium pion state. As a result, the in-medium Glashow-Weinberg relation for the charged pions cannot be derived in isospin-asymmetric nuclear matter from operator relations in quantum chromodynamics.

papers.title: Cybersecurity Practices in Industrial Automation and Control Systems: a Study of Croatian System Integrators
papers.summary: Given the increasing frequency of industrial cybersecurity incidents, governments, industry, and the research community are all working to find ways to protect industrial automation and control systems (IACSs). A key regulatory effort in the European context is the EU's Network and Information Security Directive 2 (NIS2), which aims to strengthen cybersecurity requirements and improve resilience across critical and important sectors. Nevertheless, translating cybersecurity requirements into practical engineering remains challenging within IACS environments. This paper explores how Croatian IACS system integrators perceive cybersecurity requirements, implementation challenges, and current practices in the industrial environments in which they operate. The findings are based on three focus groups with system integrators working with clients in the energy, chemical and pharmaceutical, and food and beverage sectors. Participants reported limited cybersecurity awareness among IACS owners, as well as perceived differences in practices between smaller and larger companies and between domestic and foreign firms. Participants were divided in their expectations regarding regulatory pressure: while some believed it could improve cybersecurity, others expected only minimal compliance focused on cost reduction. The results of this study provide a basis for developing more practical cybersecurity practices and offer a deeper understanding of the key challenges faced by IACS system integrators and owners when dealing with cybersecurity.

papers.title: RV2GC: Reconstructing the Garbling Boundary in a RISC-V Garbled Processor
papers.summary: Programmable garbled-circuit execution must balance the benefits of cross-program reuse against the cost of repeated work during secure execution. A complete garbled processor provides a fixed circuit for many programs, but its evaluator repeatedly visits processor-wide structures even when only a small part performs the current protected computation. We present RV2GC, which reconstructs the garbling boundary around a fixed library of RISC-V instruction circuits. Public scheduling and operand routing operate outside the circuit topologies; persistent label-encoded state connects independently invoked garbled instruction circuits and instruction-specific garbling-free paths through a common interface. A Conditional-execution Stack and protected commits support secret-dependent branches, bounded loops, and secret-indexed memory access under public scheduling, keeping instruction and memory-address sequences independent of private inputs. Across nine benchmarks, measured ARM2GC-to-RV2GC runtime ratios range from 12.81 to 4,043. In terms of circuit size, the largest listed instruction circuit has 3,386 gates, corresponding to 2.044% and 0.393% of the 256-byte and 4,096-byte Amber processors, respectively. Additional comparisons quantify schedule storage, communication, and the cost of secret-dependent execution.

papers.title: Generative artificial intelligence prompting strategies among Chinese university students across academic tasks
papers.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly embedded in university learning, yet effective human-GenAI interaction depends not only on access to these tools but also on students' ability to formulate, evaluate, and refine prompts for academic tasks. This study examined university students' perceived GenAI prompting capability and reported prompting strategies. Questionnaire data from 234 students were analyzed using descriptive statistics, measurement modelling, scenario comparisons, structural associations, and qualitative coding of optional comments. Students reported using GenAI across diverse academic activities and generally expressed confidence in their prompting capabilities, particularly in providing relevant context and refining prompts following initial outputs. However, prompting strategies showed limited sensitivity to task types: specifying output format was more strongly endorsed in a creative workshop preparation scenario than in a research-oriented assignment, whereas other matched strategies showed no adjusted differences. Students also commonly endorsed both concise instructions and providing all relevant information at the outset, suggesting that effective brevity may depend more on selecting and organizing task-relevant information than on prompt length alone. By contrast, fixed prompt templates received lower endorsement than other prompting strategies. In the adopted factor model, perceived cognition showed the clearest unique association with perceived prompting capability, while open-ended responses highlighted prompt-intent alignment as a common challenge.

papers.title: Beyond Preference Following: Benchmarking Profile-Query Arbitration in Personalized Text Transformation
papers.summary: Writing assistants use persistent preferences to personalize responses, but these can conflict with the current request. Responses can meet every requirement yet serve the task poorly, while task failures need not involve following a conflicting preference. We introduce Profile Conflict Arbitration (PCA-Bench), a benchmark of 64 rewriting tasks and 256 task-preference pairs. We construct these pairs by varying the profile preference for each fixed text and request, covering different relations between the preference and the request. We assess whether responses meet requirements, how well they achieve the request's goals, and whether they follow preferences. Across three LLMs, we find that when preferences compete with task goals, a higher success rate in meeting both requirements and preferences does not mean better responses: it can come with a greater quality loss compared with responses without a profile. Similar rates of preference following do not imply the same ability to meet the current task's requirements when preferences conflict with them.

papers.title: Judging Before Propagation: Task-Graph Contextual Integrity for Multi-Agent Privacy
papers.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on persistent memory and inter-agent communication. These capabilities create privacy risks that extend beyond individual interactions: a release appropriate in isolation may become inappropriate when combined with information previously disclosed to a recipient or propagated to downstream agents along the planned workflow. Existing Contextual Integrity (CI) mechanisms for agentic systems typically rely on local judgments that assess each disclosure in isolation, with or without regard to the recipient's history, but do not account for how information propagates downstream. However, compliance at the current boundary does not guarantee appropriateness across the workflow. We introduce Task-Graph Contextual Integrity (TG-CI), to our knowledge the first task-graph-native formalization of Contextual Integrity for multi-agent systems. TG-CI represents a workflow as a Multi-Agent Task Graph (MATG) and extends CI from atomic transfers to stateful, graph-level information flows by jointly considering an item's intended propagation scope and recipients' evolving disclosure states. We operationalize TG-CI through propagation-scoped authorization under two complementary policies: Full-Scope, which requires admissibility across the complete downstream scope, and Auto-Region, which confines each item to its maximal admissible region using lightweight frontier gates. We further introduce MAPLE-Bench, a benchmark of 144 cases across four scenarios that jointly vary MATG topology, disclosure history, compromised-agent placement, and item-level privacy policies. In our primary experimental configuration, TG-CI reduces the mean unauthorized disclosure count by 85.8-94.1% relative to the Local-History CI baseline, while retaining 93.6-96.1% of the baseline's task accuracy, with the two enforcement policies providing complementary privacy--cost--utility trade-offs.

papers.title: Systematic Evaluation of Adversarial Jailbreaking Attacks and Defenses Across Seven Large Language Models
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in safety-critical settings must resist adversarial inputs designed to elicit harmful outputs. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of five adversarial jailbreaking attack families---direct requests, roleplay-based jailbreaking, hypothetical framing, instruction override, and obfuscation---across seven open-weight and API-accessible LLMs: Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B, and Phi-4-14B. We further evaluate four defense mechanisms: keyword blacklisting, self-reminder prompting, paraphrase-based sanitization, and perplexity-based filtering against the two most vulnerable models. Our results reveal that obfuscation attacks achieve a mean attack success rate (ASR) of 54.3% across all models and constitute the most transferable adversarial vector, bypassing every evaluated model with nonzero success. We find that model size does not predict adversarial robustness (Spearman r=-0.57, p=0.18), and that models within the same architecture family exhibit dramatically different vulnerability profiles. Self-reminder prompting achieves the most consistent defense, reducing ASR from 44% to 10% on Mistral-7B and from 48% to 5% on Llama-3.1-8B with zero false positives and no additional inference cost. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Mdniloykhan/jailbreak-eval-7llms.

papers.title: When Static Reachability Says No: Checking Joern-Based Negative Verdicts for Python Against Execution
papers.summary: A negative reachability verdict removes a finding from human review. We check such verdicts against execution. Our pipeline, SourceLens, maps Semgrep findings to a Python program's call graph, whose edges a query takes from the calls that Joern links in its code property graph. We ran two command-line programs from the PyCG macro-benchmark, in which the benchmark's manual call graph and Joern disagree, under coverage and recorded the calls between their functions. On these edges, 123 functions of asciinema are unreachable from the program's entry points. The project's own integration script executes 86 of them, and all our runs 113. In Sublist3r, 19 of 24 are executed. The latest Joern release gives the same verdicts. The missing calls go through values, such as classes and functions passed around, or have no call expression, as in with blocks and property reads. In asciinema, four missing edges make 50 of the 113 executed functions reachable. The manual call graphs also lack observed calls, in asciinema many of them property reads and with blocks, which the benchmark may not count as calls. A rule that turns negative verdicts into unknown recovers 62 of the 113 and 15 of the 19, mostly through dunder and private method names. It recovers 0 of the 5 security findings with a negative verdict, all in executed functions. Its selectivity cannot be measured, as only 10 and 5 negative verdicts were not executed, and under library entry-point models it degrades every negative verdict.

papers.title: InterA11y: Interactive Web Accessibility Error Detection with LLM Agents
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential to expand the coverage of web accessibility evaluation. However, current LLM-based checkers neglect much of the interactive and dynamic web contexts, resulting in limited coverage, high false discovery rates, and inconsistent performance across models. We present InterA11y, an agentic accessibility evaluation system that combines rubrics and interactive tools to support LLM agents in evaluating accessibility effectively. The rubrics decompose WCAG success criteria (SC) into testable aspects and guide agents in collecting and interpreting evidence. The interactive tools inspect or operate a webpage deterministically to collect evidence, such as focus appearances and error messages. We developed these rubrics and tools on 682 curated test cases grounded in established accessibility guidelines that target 10 commonly violated SC. We evaluated InterA11y on 197 expert-annotated cases sampled from 54 real webpages. Results show InterA11y achieves higher recall than the strongest evaluated LLM-driven baseline (79.0% vs. 44.4%), while maintaining comparable precision to best rule-based checkers (93.1% vs. 90.3-97.6%), with little variability between models. Further, when equipped with our interactive tools, general-purpose web agents detect more accessibility errors with fewer false positives and less token usage than without these tools.
papers.comment: We release our code and data at https://github.com/jszh/InterA11y

papers.title: Does Federated Training Degrade Explainability? A Comparative Analysis of Grad-CAM Faithfulness in Centralized vs. Federated Deepfake Detection
papers.summary: Automated detection has become the essential safeguard against realistic synthetic media, but deploying it at scale requires training on sensitive data from multiple organizations, putting privacy and the transparency demanded by forensic review in direct conflict. Federated learning resolves the privacy side by sharing only model updates rather than raw data, but whether this comes at the cost of trustworthy gradient-based explanations, which analysts rely on to decide whether or not to trust a flagged clip, has not been studied. We present the systematic study of Grad-CAM explanation faithfulness under federated deepfake detection, evaluating an EfficientNet-B4 detector on FaceForensics++ across five federated clients under varying degrees of data heterogeneity. We find that the relationship between federation and explanation quality is non-monotonic: at near-IID (Independent and Identically Distributed Data) and moderate heterogeneity, federated models match or exceed the faithfulness of a centralized baseline, but at extreme heterogeneity, explanations break down entirely, becoming spatially incoherent and, on average, causally misleading. This degradation is not a general cost of federated training but a threshold effect tied to client heterogeneity, and we offer practical guidance for identifying when privacy-preserving deepfake detection can be deployed safely and when its explanations can no longer be trusted. Code and data partitions are available for reproducibility.
papers.comment: 10 Pages, 3 figures, Muhammad Uzair Shahid and Muhammad Zabil Mehboob contributed equally to this work

papers.title: GraspPressure: Understanding Pressure Input With Busy Hands
papers.summary: In many real-world scenarios, users interact with digital systems while their hands are partially occupied, such as when holding tools or everyday objects. Prior work on busy-hand interaction has focused on microgestures and motion-based techniques, which rely on finger articulation or relative movement. In situations where a stable grasp is required, such as handling fragile, heavy, or precision objects, such motion can be undesirable or impractical. Pressure-based input offers a complementary modality that enables interaction without changing finger pose, yet its use while holding objects has received limited empirical attention. To explore this, we conducted two within-subject experiments examining users' ability to perform controlled pressure selections and analyzing finger-specific performance across different grasps and geometries. Results indicate that participants can reliably perform pressure-based selections in these conditions, achieving high success rates (92.7% on average) with low selection times (1.74s on average). Our findings characterize the potential of pressure input as a complementary microinteraction modality under grasp-constrained, busy-hand scenarios.
papers.comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (PACM HCI), presented at ACM Interactive Surfaces and Spaces (ISS 2026), Turin, Italy, November 23-26, 2026

papers.title: Early-Buyer Groups and Fast-Wallet Teams on a Bonding-Curve Launchpad: A Prospective Measurement Study of pump.fun on Solana
papers.summary: We study coordinated groups of wallets on a bonding-curve launchpad (pump.fun on Solana), using a complete record of 200\,443 token launches, 15\,854\,121 curve trades and 51\,025\,958 SOL transfers over 88.3 hours. A prospective, multi-channel discovery procedure (co-buying, shared funding, joint signing, transfers, consolidation) yields 23\,710 wallet groups. Without ground-truth labels we validate them by out-of-sample link prediction, independent non-trading links and a comparison with naive co-buy clustering at equal numbers of flagged tokens: raw clustering collapses into one giant component, yet it ranks tokens at least as well as the groups, so the value of the structure is descriptive. Group activity is highly concentrated and splits into serial creators and long-lived rings of early buyers. Known members buy earlier than other buyers of the same token and extract more cash than an activity-matched placebo set, while late buyers' net cash flow is negative; tokens with members show a pump-like price path, but the contrast vanishes when controls are restricted to comparable tokens, so we report it as an association. A follower entering at the earliest group signal loses money out of sample in all 32 configurations and does no better than random entry. A few pools of tens to over a hundred fast wallets are associated with a two- to four-fold higher chance of reaching 20 SOL, also within creators, with a smaller excess at 60 SOL and none for graduation; on a final hold-out the team rules keep a precision of about one half to three quarters, yet many signals arrive when the curve already holds 20 SOL, one team supplies most of them, and they add no information beyond early curve state. We also document evaluation errors that turn the same data into apparent profit.

papers.title: Challenge or Pass? A Dynamic Policy for MLB's Automated Ball-Strike System
papers.summary: Under Major League Baseball's automated ball-strike (ABS) challenge system, players must weigh the value of overturning a call against the risk of losing a challenge they may need later. We develop a policy that values an overturn through its effect on expected runs, accounting for the count, outs, and runners on base. Using pitch tracking and game records, we reconstruct challenge opportunities, including calls that players let stand. A Bayesian model represents players' imperfect impressions of pitch location and uses them to estimate overturn probabilities, with uncertainty calibrated from historical challenge decisions. Dynamic programming compares the expected gain with the future cost of losing a challenge, accounting for the stage of the game, the number of challenges remaining, and opportunities on both offense and defense. We develop the policy using games before the 2026 All-Star break and evaluate it without refitting on 983 games played afterward. Along the recorded sequence of opportunities, the policy recovers 0.536 modeled correction runs per game across both teams, compared with 0.452 under observed decisions, an improvement of 18.5%. The gain is 0.084 runs per game, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [0.065, 0.103]. The policy makes more challenges and recovers more value per successful review despite a lower overturn rate. These results show why overturn rate alone can be a misleading measure of challenge strategy.

papers.title: ARBITRA: Robust Document-Level ATT&CK Extraction via Multi-Expert Argumentation
papers.summary: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reports describe adversary behavior in natural language, but converting them into structured MITRE ATT&CK mappings remains difficult: existing methods decompose reports to sentence-level granularity for extraction, while modern LLMs can work with full reports in a single pass but with noticeable performance degradation. We present ARBITRA, which orchestrates multiple role-specialized LLM experts that propose candidate ATT&CK entities from the full report, which are then verified through a per-candidate quantitative bipolar argumentation framework (QBAF) grounded in document evidence and rationales. We additionally construct reasoning-specialized corpora for fine-tuning so experts can act as effective participants during this verification process. Across ATT&CK extraction benchmarks, ARBITRA reaches a stronger precision-oriented operating point than sentence-level pipelines, recent LLM-based extraction systems, and frontier models including GPT-5.5. Under adversarial perturbations simulating conflicting TTP statements, cross-report contamination, and semantic poisoning, ARBITRA limits mean precision degradation to roughly half that of frontier-model baselines for a more robust extraction.
papers.comment: 13 pages of main paper, 21 pages total, preprint

papers.title: Nonlinear Sufficient Dimension Reduction for Causal Inference with Continuous Treatments
papers.summary: Causal inference with continuous treatments requires estimating nuisance functions to adjust for the potentially high-dimensional confounder, but nonparametric estimation of these functions is severely hampered by the curse of dimensionality. To address this challenge, we propose a nonlinear sufficient dimension reduction framework to construct low-dimensional sufficient confounders to preserve the unbiasedness of the treatment effect. We estimate the causal effect by combining the generalized Sliced Inverse Regression with the inverse probability weighting, outcome regression, and augmented inverse probability weighting, respectively. We further establish the convergence rates of the first two estimators and derive the asymptotic distributions of the third. Our theoretical results show that, compared to estimators based on the full covariates, dimension reduction yields faster convergence rates and weaker rate conditions without inflating the asymptotic variance. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed estimators improve finite-sample performance over their counterparts without dimension reduction, particularly when the original covariate dimension is high. These results demonstrate that sufficient dimension reduction provides a flexible approach to mitigating the curse of dimensionality in causal inference with continuous treatments.

papers.title: Self-normalised change point tests that remain pivotal under non-stationarity
papers.summary: Self-normalising test statistics for time series circumvent the lag-specification of long-run variance estimators by employing an inconsistent estimator for studentization. This leads to asymptotically pivotal test distributions under stationarity, but not for nonstationary sequences. Focusing on the multiple changepoint problem, we propose an alternative self-normalised test statistic which is asymptotically pivotal even if the noise is nonstationary. Central to our argument are statistical functionals which are invariant under temporal reparametriation, i.e. clock-changes. Simulations show that the proposed procedure is more conservative than competing bootstrap procedures, but considerably more powerful against multiple changes and more reliable in terms of size for highly nonstationary time series in larger samples.
papers.comment: Keywords: Changepoint testing, nonstationarity, temporal dependence, self-normalisation

papers.title: Absorption of bound supernova axion-like particles by the neutron star weakens the heating limits on their photon coupling
papers.summary: Axion-like particles (ALPs) that couple to protons are produced in a core-collapse supernova, and the slow ones remain bound to the new neutron star. Bose, Ganguly, Kumar, and Raj [arXiv:2610.30255] proposed that the photons from the decay of this bound cloud reheat old neutron stars, and they derived strong limits on the ALP-photon coupling. They neglected the absorption of the ALPs by the star, but a bound ALP on an orbit that enters the star and reaches 50 km crosses it about $6\times 10^{18}$ times over the 333 Myr age of PSR J2144$-$3933. We show that inverse nucleon bremsstrahlung in the cold star absorbs every ALP whose orbit enters it within minutes, long before it decays, so only ALPs born outside the final star on nearly circular orbits survive; they carry $9\times 10^{-9} - 6\times 10^{-5}$ of the heating. We compute the protoneutron-star evolution, the production, the general-relativistic orbits and the absorption ourselves, for twelve protoneutron-star evolutions, three nucleon-bremsstrahlung rates normalized to the same supernova energy loss of light ALPs, and equations of state with and without $Δ(1232)$ isobars. PSR J2144$-$3933 still excludes a window at $m_a\simeq 7.7-196$\ MeV, with a lower edge in the photon coupling $280-700$ times higher than without absorption. Pion conversion and the $Δ(1232)$ resonance, which raise the production of surviving ALPs more than their absorption, widen this window to $m_a\simeq$ $7.7-260$\ MeV. The window depends at similar levels on the bremsstrahlung rate and on the radius of the final star. It requires a direct photon coupling that cancels the one induced by ALP-pion mixing, and existing supernova gamma-ray limits may already cover it.

papers.title: Optimal fiber comparisons for random tensors
papers.summary: We extend Seginer's matrix norm comparison to tensors with optimal dependence on the tensor order. For a real tensor $T$ of order $k\ge2$ with centered, integrable, independent and identically distributed entries, we prove $\mathbb{E} f(T)\le\mathbb{E}\lVert T\rVert_{\mathrm{inj}} \le C\sqrt{k\log k}\,\mathbb{E} f(T)$, where $f(T)$ is the largest Euclidean norm of a one-dimensional fiber and $C$ is universal. The comparison holds for every finite rectangular format, and the entry law may depend on both the dimensions and the tensor order. We show that the factor $\sqrt{k\log k}$ is optimal by considering Rademacher tensors on $[2]^k$.

papers.title: What is Work For? Labor, Politics, and Meaning in the Age of AI
papers.summary: This paper investigates the role of work in providing meaning, purpose, community, and other non-monetary benefits. Using an original cross-national survey of 8,234 working-age adults across the UK, US, Denmark, and India, I study the factors that motivate people in their work, with an eye toward the future AI economic transformation. I find that 81% of respondents report being satisfied with their job, and a majority across all four countries are strongly motivated by the non-monetary components of their employment. Using an original "Work Values" Index, I show that one third of working respondents are motivated intrinsically by their job--valuing their role for its own sake. Nearly one quarter are driven by social and community-related aspects of their employment, 17% by social status, and just over one quarter by the transactional financial benefits of their job. Although a majority of people would leave their role if offered their current salary as a guaranteed income, one fifth of workers would stay even if offered up to 120% of their salary. Intrinsically motivated workers were disproportionately likely to refuse a basic income at any substitution level. Groups attached to their job for non-monetary reasons were also more likely to pursue volunteering or work-like activities if they received guaranteed income substitution but could no longer perform their role. Crucially, these non-monetary work motivations are evenly distributed across the income distribution and between white- and blue-collar workers. I argue that these findings have implications for managing the AI transition, understanding attitudes to AI, and making sense of policy preferences. Guaranteeing a basic income may indeed be necessary for managing any future AI labor shock, yet it could ultimately fail to compensate workers for any loss of the non-monetary benefits they derive from work.

papers.title: DualGuard: Comprehensive and Efficient Memory Safety across Sequential and Speculative Execution
papers.summary: Although decades of research have yielded sophisticated mechanisms for enforcing memory safety, speculative execution can subvert these protections through transient memory operations. Conversely, defenses designed specifically for speculative safety, such as Speculative Load Hardening (SLH), cannot enforce memory safety during non-speculative execution. A naive combination of defenses from both domains raises two fundamental challenges: (1) which combination of otherwise fragmented defenses can ensure dual memory safety under speculative and non-speculative executions? (2) whether such combinations introduce redundant protections that incur unnecessary performance overhead? We present DualGuard, a unified framework for dual memory protection under non-speculative and speculative executions. DualGuard systematically analyzes memory behaviors, classifying them into four categories, and further identifies the minimal composition requirements for dual memory safety, which allow us to strategically combine existing mitigations and design new ones to avoid redundant or excessive protections. We implement DualGuard through a combination of static analysis and runtime enforcement within the LLVM infrastructure. Our evaluation demonstrates that DualGuard reduces overhead by 3%-72% compared to naive compositions of fragmented defenses. In some cases, it even incurs lower overhead than approaches that guarantee memory safety solely under either non-speculative or speculative execution.

papers.title: Lookover: Scaffolding Student Participation in Social Annotation
papers.summary: Social annotation platforms such as Perusall and Hypothesis are widely used to support student engagement with course readings, often through required commenting. Yet visible participation does not necessarily produce sustained or substantive peer exchange. Analyzing six weeks of Perusall activity from a graduate course (2,873 comments), we found that participation was often fragmented: 53.5% of comments received no reply, 38.3% were posted within the final 12 hours before the deadline, and over one-third of a double-coded sample went no further than repeating or agreeing with the reading or a peer. Interviews pointed to two linked difficulties: locating a discussion worth entering and contributing something that meaningfully advances it. We present Lookover, an AI-assisted annotation system that scaffolds both stages without writing for students. Discussion Overview helps students identify active themes and relevant threads, while Spark Thinking poses questions that encourage them to move beyond reaction and restatement toward questioning, extending, and substantively responding to peers. A preliminary study with five participants found Discussion Overview valuable for those who noticed it, while the usefulness of Spark Thinking depended on how much a participant already knew about the topic.
papers.comment: 3 pages, 1 figure. Poster at UIST Adjunct 2026, the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, November 2-5, 2026, Detroit, MI, USA

papers.title: Irreducible representations of $SU(3)$ for nucleons in a oscillator shell $η$ with $η\le 8$: Application to nuclei with proxy-$SU(4)$ symmetry
papers.summary: Applying some simple rules, established in group theory literature, generated are codes (easy to modify as required) for obtaining $SU(3)$ irreducible representations (irreps) for a given number of nucleons in a given oscillator shell $η$ with $η\le 8$. In this approach, first the $SU(3)$ irreps are obtained for spinless fermions in a given $η$ shell. Using the codes developed, tables of $SU(3)$ irreps are generated for identical nucleons (protons or neutrons) with a given total spin $S$. Similarly, the $SU(3)$ irreps are generated for nucleons with a given spin-isospin $SU(4)$ irrep. Some applications of these tables for $η=4$ shell for $52 \le \mbox{Z,N} \le 78$ nuclei with proxy-$SU(4)$ symmetry are presented. Also, the procedure used for the shell model $SU(3)$ limits is easy to be extended for the $SU(3)$ limit of various interacting boson models and some examples for these are also presented.
papers.comment: 34 pages, 14 tables, 4 figures, article based on the talk given in SDANCA-2026 held in Sofia (Bulgaria) in September 2026

papers.title: Measuring Duplication, Leakage, and Rendering Dependence in Malware-as-Image Benchmarks
papers.summary: Classifying malware binaries rendered as images is a popular approach to malware family identification, and papers on the standard benchmarks for this task report accuracies of 97-99%. In this paper we audit ten of these benchmarks for near-duplicate images and test-train leakage, and retrain standard classifiers under naive and content-aware splits. Deduplicating by file hash, which is the standard practice, does not prevent leakage, because distinct binaries render to identical images. Deduplicating on image content reduces top-1 accuracy by up to 8 points and macro-F1 by up to 15 points on the released benchmarks we find leaky. The rendering step also adds duplication, since byteplots of the same binaries contain 19.7% near-duplicates where static feature vectors contain 2.2%, and changing the width at which bytes are wrapped into rows reduces accuracy by 20 to 33 points, although no byte changes. We recommend that content-level duplication and a non-image baseline be reported alongside accuracy.

papers.title: Does the Citation Matter? Quality, Grounding, and Physician-Rubric Accuracy of Google's AI Overviews for Medical Information
papers.summary: Google's AI Overviews (AIOs) are the first result users encounter when searching the web, shifting the work of selecting and evaluating sources from the user to Gemini. This may be especially consequential for health information, given that Google's traditional algorithm was designed to prioritize quality sources, and inaccurate information carries health risks. We evaluated 3,611 benchmark health questions, comparing each AIO against that question's top five traditional results on source selection and quality. We also evaluated the AIOs' statement grounding in their cited sources and how accurate AIOs were against physician-written rubrics. Overviews appeared for 96.4% of questions but drew on substantially different evidence than traditional search: only 44.4% of the top five results were cited by the corresponding AIO, which instead overrepresented commercial health publishers (e.g., WebMD, Healthline) at the expense of academic and government sources (e.g., Cleveland Clinic, National Health Service). AIO-cited pages scored lower than traditional results on four of six well-established credibility criteria. The grounding of AIO statements to their sources was poor: after correcting for classifier error, an estimated 56.7% of cited statements were supported by their cited page, and a further 20.8% of all statements were factual claims with no citation at all. When AIOs were graded against physicians' rubrics, they earned 38.2% of all available points (e.g., accuracy 54.2%, completeness 21.6%), and among the subset of AIOs whose physician rubric anticipated a specific inaccurate or potentially harmful claim, 22.2% of AIOs contained the harmful content. Notably, the accuracy of AIOs was unrelated to the grounding of their statements. We recommend AIO literacy interventions for users and holding AIOs at least to Google's own health-ranking standards.
papers.comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/SamAgnoli/AIOverviews

papers.title: Weighted Score Matching on Bounded Domains: Nonparametric Density Estimation and Interaction Graph Recovery
papers.summary: We study nonparametric density estimation and interaction-graph recovery on bounded product domains using boundary-weighted score matching. In a canonically centered pairwise log-density model, graph edges are determined by bivariate interactions, but penalizing the univariate main effects can induce false edges. We derive the resulting shift in interaction scores and study partially penalized weighted score matching (P-WSM), which leaves main effects unpenalized. At the population level, P-WSM excludes edges between independent subsystems even when the marginal log densities are not represented exactly by the sieve. A nonparametric construction separates partial and joint penalization: throughout a common deterministic tuning interval, P-WSM recovers the graph while joint penalization selects a false edge. We also give growing-dimensional recovery conditions that do not require full-Gram invertibility. For density estimation at fixed dimension, we establish weighted Fisher-divergence rates and, under stronger basis-specific conditions, Kullback-Leibler and Hellinger rates for the normalized estimator. Simulations examine the benefits and limitations of partial penalization. An analysis of bone-marrow signaling data illustrates nonlinear conditional-association estimation.

papers.title: Neutron Optical Constraints on Exotic Parity-odd Interactions between Neutrons and Nucleons
papers.summary: Many theories beyond the standard model of particle physics predict the existence of weakly-coupled exotic spin-dependent interactions between standard model particles. We use experimental upper bounds on neutron-nucleus parity violation at meV and keV neutron energies in the forward scattering limit described by neutron optics to constrain exotic parity-odd interactions of the neutron with nucleons from exotic vector boson exchange for force ranges between $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-14}$ meters.
papers.comment: 12 pages, 2 figures; submitted to Physical Review C

papers.title: Independence tests of general spatial point processes based on characteristic functions
papers.summary: Existing nonparametric tests of spatial point process independence typically rely on random shifts to simulate their null distributions. This limits their scope to stationary point processes in rectangular study regions. Attempts to adapt random shift methods to nonrectangular study regions have resulted in significant power loss. We introduce a new type of nonparametric independence tests by taking differences of several characteristic-function-based goodness-of-fit statistics. We develop two null distribution methods for the tests without using random shifts, by making normal or symmetry assumptions on the Mercer's expansion of the test statistics. The methods are applicable to general nonstationary point processes in study regions of any shape. In simulations, our tests based on the symmetric null distribution method have better type I error control and higher power than toroidal cross-$K$ tests in most scenarios where toroidal shifts can be applied. When tested on more general settings given appropriately-fitted marginal distributions, they still have good power and almost always control the type I error well.

papers.title: TwinPoSI: Statistical Twins for Powerful Post-Selection Inference on Population-Based Regression Coefficients
papers.summary: Post-selection inference (PoSI) quantifies uncertainty about regression coefficients after data-driven feature selection. A central question is the inferential target. Projection-based targets are the coefficients of the best linear approximation restricted to the selected features and depend on the selection procedure, whereas population-based targets are the selected features' coefficients in the full linear model and are often more relevant for scientific interpretation. The two targets can differ, even in sign. Existing PoSI methods largely focus on projection-based targets and may yield overly wide confidence intervals. We propose TwinPoSI (statistical twin post-selection inference), a method for powerful PoSI on population-based targets with false coverage rate (FCR) control. TwinPoSI leverages \textit{statistical twins}, defined as synthetic datasets generated from a fitted model to mimic the original data. With generating parameters known, statistical twins enable direct calibration of confidence intervals for bias introduced by data-dependent feature selection. We establish that TwinPoSI controls the FCR at the nominal level, up to Monte Carlo error and an asymptotically negligible approximation error. Moreover, in a Gaussian linear model with an orthogonal design, TwinPoSI uniquely attains the oracle average interval length to first order among the methods considered. Simulations show that TwinPoSI maintains reliable FCR control for both population-based and projection-based targets while yielding shorter confidence intervals and higher power than the competing methods. In riboflavin production data, TwinPoSI identifies associated genes, quantifies their directions and magnitudes of association, and yields the shortest average intervals among the methods considered.

papers.title: Effects of the $a_0(980)$ Meson on Finite Nuclei in a Parity Doublet Model
papers.summary: We investigate nuclear structure within the parity doublet model (PDM), with particular emphasis on the role of the isovector-scalar $a_0(980)$ meson. We adopt the models with and without the $a_0$ meson and fit their parameters to nuclear matter saturation and ground state properties of selected nuclei, subject to constraints from the vacuum. The resulting parameter sets reproduce the nuclear matter saturation properties and provide a good description of binding energies and charge radii of selected nuclei. Our fits show that a large value of the chiral invariant mass of nucleon is preferred by the fitting: the best fitted value is $m_0 = 689 \pm 71 $ MeV with $a_0$ and $m_0 = 689 \pm 69 $ MeV without $a_0$. We find that the effects of the $a_0$ meson on the binding energies and charge radii are negligibly small. It is difficult to clarify the effect of $a_0$ meson to neutron skin thickness of Sn, Pb, and Ca isotopes, due to the large uncertainty of the predictions. We note that our prediction of $^{208} \text{Pb}$ is consistent with the measurement by PREX-II collaboration, while that of $^{48} \text{Ca}$ cannot explain the CREX result.

papers.title: Bregman projections and partition design for accelerating finite Markov chains
papers.summary: We study Gibbs averaging of finite Markov chains with a prescribed stationary distribution $π$. Given a transition matrix $P$ and the Gibbs kernel $G$ induced by a state-space partition, we prove that $GPG$ is an information projection for every admissible Bregman generator $φ$, with divergences defined using transition probabilities relative to $π$. A Pythagorean identity characterizes this projection and recovers the relative entropy and weighted Frobenius cases. A dual characterization identifies $GPG$ as a kernel closest to stationarity among those with the same projection chain as $P$; for relative entropy, it maximizes the entropy rate. The identities also give monotonicity under partition coarsening. For every reversible ergodic baseline $P$, Gibbs averaging cannot increase the squared weighted Frobenius distance to stationarity at any positive integer time, and the inequality is strict unless $P=GPG$. The corresponding mixing time therefore cannot increase. To choose the partition, we identify the divergence of $G$ from stationarity as the exact worst-case divergence of $GPG$ over all $π$-stationary baselines $P$. This objective depends only on the block masses. We give an exact algorithm for concave block costs, including those arising from relative entropy and power generators $φ(u)=u^p$ with $1<p<2$, and a greedy approximation algorithm with a provable guarantee for $p>2$. For power generators $φ(u)=u^p$ with $p>1$, the objective is proportional to Tsallis entropy of order $2-p$: its minimization favors imbalanced block masses when $1<p<2$ and balanced block masses when $p>2$, while all $k$-block partitions have the same objective value when $p=2$. A numerical experiment compares the resulting projected chains with a local Metropolis sampler on a multi-modal $π$.

papers.title: AgentHeal: Evaluating Goal-Preserving Resource Recovery of Web Agents under Access Barriers
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in automating complex information-seeking and transactional tasks across the open web. However, their real-world reliability remains limited by access barriers, such as dead links, authentication walls, rate limits, and anti-scraping defenses. These barriers block the primary execution path, causing agents to abort prematurely, loop indefinitely, or quietly compromise the user's original constraints. Existing evaluations either implicitly assume that target resources are freely accessible or focus on transient perturbations that simple retries can resolve, failing to capture scenarios where agents must actively reroute around impassable bottlenecks. To bridge this gap, this paper introduces AgentHeal, a comprehensive benchmark evaluating goal-preserving resource recovery, defined as the ability of web agents to detect non-transient access barriers, pivot to legitimate alternative sources, and fulfill the user's exact original objective. Spanning nine barrier families across a counterfactual sandbox and real-website replay, our experiments on leading LLM backbones show that average task success drops sharply from 89.4% to 43.7% under access barriers. Further analysis reveals that agents frequently fall for deceptive look-alikes, fail to escalate to users when necessary, violate access policies, or waste computation on futile retries, providing actionable diagnostics for developing resilient web agents.
papers.comment: Code and Dataset are available at https://github.com/Lzzzzzzzzzzy/AgentHeal

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders as Implicit Diversification Regularisers for Cross-Sectional Cryptocurrency Returns
papers.summary: Factor models are central to asset pricing and portfolio construction, but neural factors are often difficult to interpret, and their effect on portfolio risk is unclear. A sparse autoencoder (SAE) may address both concerns by describing daily returns across many assets with only a few active features. We ask whether this sparse representation produces stable financial factors and better-diversified portfolios. We study cryptocurrency returns, use equities as a secondary test, and compare the SAE with common benchmarks in a time-ordered evaluation. We find consistently lower volatility in SAE portfolios and link this result to lower correlations among the selected assets. However, the SAE does not outperform a simple contrarian strategy on risk-adjusted return, and its factor identities are not stable across training runs. Our contribution is to show that sparse coding can support portfolio diversification, while clearly separating this risk effect from claims about alpha or stable factor identities.
papers.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the 7th ACM International Conference on AI in Finance (ICAIF '26)

papers.title: Enhanced structure-dependent alpha decay tunneling in deformed odd-odd nuclei via intense two-color laser pulses
papers.summary: In the present work, we investigate the effect of ultra-intense laser fields on the $α$ decay tunneling of deformed odd-odd nuclei. Calculations performed within the deformed density-dependent cluster model show that, for deformed odd-odd $α$ emitters, the laser-induced variation in the penetration probability separates into distinct branches associated with different valence particle-hole configurations relative to the $Z=82$ and $N=126$ shell closures. In contrast to the even-even and odd-$A$ cases, the odd-odd parent nucleus most sensitive to the laser field is not the one with the lowest $α$ decay energy. This indicates that the laser response is governed not only by $Q_α$ but also by structural correlations associated with the simultaneously unpaired proton and neutron. We further examine the pulse-averaged response under a two-color laser field. The results show that an optimized two-color field enhances the pulse-averaged laser response for most of the studied nuclei, while highly sensitive nuclei exhibit an effective gain equivalent to increasing the laser intensity by more than one order of magnitude. These findings identify structural determinants of laser-assisted $α$ decay in odd-odd nuclei and provide guidance for selecting candidate nuclei and optimizing laser parameters in future experiments.

papers.title: Persistence of Bounded Rationality in Financial Markets: An Evolutionary Game-Theoretic Model
papers.summary: Classical theory predicts that irrational traders lose money to rational traders and are eventually driven out of the market. Yet noise trading, herding, and heuristic trading persist even in highly developed markets. We model a financial market as an ecology of two trading-behavior types, relatively rational (R) and boundedly rational (N), whose composition evolves under replicator dynamics according to relative performance. Each type's fitness depends on the share of the other type and on frictions. When the interaction is complementary, that is, rational traders profit from the mispricing created by boundedly rational traders while the latter benefit from the liquidity and price correction supplied by the former, and when the difference in frictions is moderate, a unique interior composition exists and is globally asymptotically stable: bounded rationality persists endogenously. When the interaction is antagonistic, the same point becomes a tipping threshold between two one-type regimes. Comparative statics show that lowering the costs of disciplined trading, as algorithmic and AI-based trading does, shifts the composition toward rational trading continuously but does not eliminate bounded rationality unless the cost advantage exceeds an explicit threshold.
papers.comment: 4 pages, 1 figure. JEL: C73, G14, G41

papers.title: Wearable Biosensors for Early Detection and Continuous Monitoring of Postpartum Depression: A Human-Centered Approach
papers.summary: Postpartum depression (PPD) is the leading cause of maternal mortality in the United States. However, there are significant gaps in PPD screening, detection, and treatment. A main challenge stems from limitations in existing methods for early PPD diagnosis and subsequent monitoring and intervention. Mobile technology that incorporates interactive interfaces and continuous wearable biosensors holds major potential to augment clinical decision-making and enhance PPD care. A number of compelling research directions exist in effectively developing such systems, including user experience design, sensing accuracy during perinatal stages, clinical integration and interoperability, acceptance and adoption, and privacy and ethics. By focusing on wearable devices that center women and their experiences, this paper discusses such challenges and opportunities at the intersections of HCI, inclusive physiological computing, and women's health.
papers.comment: 2024 PhysioCHI: Towards Best Practices for Integrating Physiological Signals in HCI

papers.title: Unlocking with the Heart: Investigating User Perceptions of ECG-Based Biometric Authentication
papers.summary: Password-based authentication remains challenging for many users, especially for those who face usability and accessibility issues. The burden of maintaining security can cause user fatigue, frustration and non-engagement. To address these issues, we conducted a pilot study to assess ECG-based biometric authentication as a passwordless alternative and to gather adult participants' perspectives on this approach. The research consisted of a survey study, an authentication prototype and a follow-up usability experience questionnaire. Our approach combined an online survey of 337 adults examining authentication practices and perceptions, with a separate usability evaluation in which 49 participants interacted with a simulated ECG-authentication and password interface in a health-care application prototype, then completed a post-test usability test questionnaire. The survey examined how adults across age groups use and perceive various authentication techniques, their experiences with biometrics, their views on security and convenience, and their willingness to adopt ECG authentication. In parallel, the usability prototype and questionnaire captured participants' responses after hands-on interaction with an ECG authentication prototype.

papers.title: The Welfare Limits of Market Segmentation with Captive Consumers
papers.summary: In a duopoly with captive and contested consumers, I characterize every pair of consumer and producer surplus that can arise under some market composition and some public segmentation, and construct a market that produces each pair. The set is lens-shaped. At any level of industry profit, consumers do worst when captive and contested consumers are perfectly separated and best in an unsegmented market in which the two firms have equally many captives. A market with unequal captive bases and some contested consumers cannot reach this upper frontier under any segmentation. Between Bertrand competition and monopoly, the frontier itself lies strictly below what consumers would get if everyone paid a single deterministic price yielding the same profit. Firms must randomize, and with downward-sloping demand the resulting price dispersion lowers consumer surplus.

papers.title: Muon-to-positron conversion from light Majorana neutrino exchange: nuclear responses and pion-pole-improved multipoles
papers.summary: We study muon-to-positron conversion in nuclei that is mediated by light Majorana neutrinos, which probes lepton-number violation in the electron-muon sector. As the second paper in a series, this work extends our study of local dimension-nine interactions to the mass mechanism. We derive the conversion amplitude from the second-order effective four-Fermi interaction and express it in terms of nuclear responses in the one-body impulse approximation. Using phenomenological nucleon form factors, we retain convection, axial charge, weak magnetism, and the longitudinal pion-pole current in a specified pion-pole-improved prescription. The two physical time orderings and the distinct momentum transfers are derived in the intermediate-state response. We complete its angular reduction and derive the corresponding closure operator, including spin-gradient terms. Both the symmetric (scalar) and antisymmetric (vector) lepton-hadron Lorentz contractions contribute to the spin-averaged, angle-integrated rate. For $0^+\!\to0^+$ transitions we give explicit formulas in terms of two coherent radial amplitudes, without restricting the intermediate nuclei to spin zero. This provides an interface to nuclear calculations of the required nuclear matrix elements. However, in this work, no isotope-specific numerical predictions are attempted. The present treatment uses approximate lepton wavefunctions and recoil-free nuclear propagation. Two-body weak currents and systematic chiral effective-field-theory matching are left for future work.

papers.title: Proton GTMDs and Wigner Distributions in the Chiral Quark Soliton Model: Orbital Angular Momentum and Spin-Orbit Correlation with Sea Quarks
papers.summary: We calculate the leading-twist vector and axial-vector quark generalized transverse-momentum-dependent distributions (GTMDs) of the proton in the chiral quark soliton model, including both the discrete valence level and the regularized Dirac sea. We consider the isosinglet and isotriplet combinations of GTMDs at zero and nonzero skewness. At zero skewness, we construct Wigner distributions and resolve the orbital angular momentum (OAM) and spin-orbit correlation (SOC) densities in transverse position and momentum space, separately for quarks and antiquarks. This provides a phase-space picture of the sea-quark and sea-antiquark contributions, displaying OAM aligned with the proton spin and anti-aligned with the partons' own spin.

papers.title: Frequency-induced Tipping: Resonance-Driven Tipping in a Threshold Predator-Prey System
papers.summary: Tipping points refer to abrupt, substantial, and often irreversible transitions in dynamic systems that can be triggered by minor perturbations. Existing tipping mechanisms are usually classified by the nature of the trigger: bifurcation-induced tipping occurs when a parameter crosses a critical threshold, noise-induced tipping is caused by random perturbations, rate-induced tipping occurs when a system fails to track a moving attractor, and phase-induced tipping is triggered by timed perturbations relative to an oscillatory state. In this paper, we identify a new mechanism for tipping: frequency-induced tipping, in which periodic forcing drives a transition through resonant amplification. This occurs by destabilization of an equilibrium via subthreshold perturbations of the appropriate frequency. Filippov analysis of a piecewise-smooth model identifies admissible crossings that lead either to predator loss or to extinction of predator and prey, and numerical simulations show that tipping persists after smoothing of the thresholds. These results extend the current tipping framework to include critical transitions under recurrent environmental forcing.

papers.title: Measuring Longer-Horizon Leveraged ETF Performance
papers.summary: Many investors hold leveraged exchange-traded funds (LETFs) for more than one day. Because these products reset leverage daily, their longer-horizon returns need not equal the stated leverage multiple times the underlying return. We explain this gap using a return identity that separates what we call the convexity bonus, volatility drag, and product costs. We also discuss several common ways to measure LETF performance and highlight how these measures can produce misleading assessments of how real-world LETFs perform. We propose evaluating ex-post performance using realized terminal wealth, which measures how much invested wealth grew. For ex-ante analysis, we propose using expected log returns to quantify how fast capital compounds over time. We show that estimating expected cumulative return by compounding the historical arithmetic mean can rank investments backwards, report gains for funds that lose money, suggest that infinite leverage is optimal when expected returns exceed borrowing cost, and reward temporary price fluctuations that reduce LETF wealth. We argue that even if the distribution of daily returns is known by the econometrician, expected terminal wealth is sensitive to whether the model draws days independently or draws monthly or annual blocks of daily returns and can be driven by a small number of economically infeasible payouts.

papers.title: Usable String Matching by Humans through Overlaid Presentation
papers.summary: We explore the ability of humans to compare strings, an error-prone activity which occurs in critical contexts (e.g., bank wire transfers), where it is not always possible to trust a machine to help. We hypothesize that understanding human cognitive and perceptual limitations can improve how people verify whether two character strings are identical. We vary the strings' relative positions and presentation formats to measure comparison speed and accuracy. We present results from two online experiments with 178 human subjects who compared pairs of strings to determine whether the two strings were identical. The strings varied by length (5 characters to small paragraphs), difference (matching versus making a random change or a hard-to-detect one), alignment (vertical versus horizontal), and presentation (Overlay versus Adjacent). Our experiments test whether, by encoding and memory tasks into perceptual tasks, overlay formats can offer advantages in speed and accuracy. Results show that overlay offers a substantially faster method, with improved accuracy for long strings. Nevertheless, mean error rates were at least 4 percent, indicating that even the improved approach may be insufficiently accurate for many verification tasks.
papers.comment: A shorter version of this paper (without the appendices) has been conditionally accepted to the International Journal of Human-Computer Studies (IJHCS)

papers.title: Configuration-Interaction Studies of Alpha Clustering in Atomic Nuclei
papers.summary: Clustering in atomic nuclei, and $α$ clustering in particular, is a striking form of self-organization in quantum many-body systems, emerging from nucleon--nucleon interactions through the interplay of correlations, symmetry constraints, and continuum coupling. We summarize a configuration-interaction approach in which cluster degrees of freedom are built from center-of-mass boosted fragment wave functions and treated with resonating-group techniques. The norm kernel plays an important role: Pauli blocking suppresses cluster channels at small separations, restructures the relative-motion wave functions, and governs the normalization of clustering strength. As the central development we present a Green's function (GF) method that aids in resolving a long-standing difficulty of harmonic-oscillator based configuration interaction calculations that stems from wave functions with Gaussian asymptotics. The method restores the correct asymptotic behavior and extracts the asymptotic normalization coefficient (ANC) with high accuracy even in very modest harmonic-oscillator spaces. The value of the ANC is very sensitive to the exact position of the state relative to threshold, and yet the GF method establishes the ANC as a structural observable that can be determined precisely from the interior wave function using the experimentally or otherwise known exact energy. A self-consistent iteration, formulated as an integral-operator eigenvalue problem, is also shown to recover both the energy and the ANC in cases when the energy of the state is to be determined. The method is illustrated for near-threshold states, such as the weakly bound $1^-$ state of $^{16}$O, as well as for the ground states of $^{16}$O and $^{20}$Ne.
papers.comment: Proceedings of CLUSTERS 2026 conference; submitted to IOP

papers.title: Capital growth since the 19th century
